subtasks.name: Extract clauses from incoming contracts
subtasks.description: The AI reads each incoming equipment-lease contract and pulls out the key clauses and the party details so they can be compared with the playbook.
subtasks.rationale: Extraction follows clear patterns and errors are caught in later review. Contracts name representatives and guarantors, so personal details are involved.

subtasks.name: Compare clauses with the clause playbook
subtasks.description: Each extracted clause is checked against the clause playbook to see whether it matches the standard position or differs from it.
subtasks.rationale: The playbook is written down, but matching wording to a standard needs some weighing. A missed difference could pass to the lawyer, so errors cause rework or delay.

subtasks.name: Flag non-standard terms
subtasks.description: Clauses that differ from the playbook, or are missing, are marked as non-standard so the lawyer can focus on them.
subtasks.rationale: Deciding what counts as non-standard draws on experience. A missed flag could lead to unfavourable terms being accepted, which is a costly business error.

subtasks.name: Recommend a position on non-standard clauses
subtasks.description: For each non-standard clause, the AI suggests a position our side could take, for the lawyer to accept, change or reject.
subtasks.rationale: Weighing risk against commercial aims is a matter on which experienced lawyers can disagree. A poor recommendation could shape contract terms. Only businesses are affected.

subtasks.name: Draft redline suggestions
subtasks.description: The AI drafts proposed edits to the contract wording, reflecting the recommended positions, for a lawyer to review.
subtasks.rationale: Drafting wording takes skill that is hard to write down. Errors that slip through could put poor terms in a contract, but the lawyer reviews the draft.

subtasks.name: Decide which positions to take
subtasks.description: A lawyer reviews the flagged clauses, recommendations and redlines, and decides which positions to take with the customer.
subtasks.rationale: This is the final judgment, weighing legal risk and business aims. A wrong call has costly effects, though it concerns business terms rather than a person's rights.

assumptions: A lawyer reviews every redline before it goes to the customer.
The clause playbook is a written document that the AI can be given.
Guarantors are named in the contract but are not the subject of any decision in this process.
Contracts are in a digital, readable format.
The AI output is a recommendation only and the lawyer makes the final decision.
clarifyingQuestions: Are guarantors assessed or decided on in this process, or only named in contracts?
How often do contracts depart from the playbook, and how is that tracked?
Does the lawyer review every clause or only the ones flagged?

confirmationEdits.reason: The recommended position sets the contract terms the organization accepts; the reviewer confirms it as the step that bears on the decision, as in the hand-confirmed preset (SPEC §10 golden tier II).

narrative.executiveSummary: The verdict is Go with conditions, at the AIA-inspired indicative tier II. BC PIPA and PIPEDA likely apply, so consider documenting a reasonable purpose and a valid form of consent, and accountability for personal information sent to an AI vendor; the OPC draft guidance suggests vendor due diligence. Splitline rates each of these an action, with the privacy officer working with the product owner or procurement as likely owners.
narrative.splitNarrative: AI does it (spot-checked) for Extract clauses from incoming contracts and Compare clauses with the clause playbook. AI drafts, a person checks and signs off for Flag non-standard terms, Recommend a position on non-standard clauses, Draft redline suggestions and Decide which positions to take. This is a starting split that the team will move as evidence comes in. The next split review is on 2026-12-26, then monthly.
leverNarratives: Who decides what the AI does: let the team doing the work choose which steps the AI does, using tools and labels shared with other teams. Keep the guardrail in place: Shared platform: common tools, common labels, and visible splits. The direct cost is some automation efficiency: you give up part of the consistency and scale you would get from one split shared by all teams.

How the team adjusts the split, and how often: the team adjusts the split as it learns, on a fixed base of data formats, hand-off points and escalation thresholds, and re-checks it monthly. Keep the guardrail in place: Standardized base: agreed data formats, handoff points, and escalation thresholds. The direct cost is some automation efficiency: the team spends attention adjusting the split, and outputs vary more above the fixed base.

How your experts and the AI team learn from each other: set up a rotating AI steward inside the team, with regular joint sessions on the system's failures and edge cases. Keep the guardrail in place: Retained differentiation: dedicated time for technical and for domain work. The direct cost is some standalone depth on each side: experts and AI specialists spend time on each other's work.
narrative.rolloutNarrative: Days 1–30, Foundation & guardrails: assign condition owners, set up the shared platform and standardized base, and publish the starting split. Days 31–60, Shadow pilot & calibration: run the AI in shadow mode and calibrate escalation thresholds. Days 61–90, Controlled scale & audit: go live in controlled increments, hold the first split review and audit a sample of decisions. KPIs: Review hours per contract; Decision quality on non-routine cases (sampled expert review); Corrections fed back into the system per month.
